# m100-silicon-binning

> An open-source analysis pipeline that recovers **per-die CPU core-harvest maps** from
> out-of-band BMC/IPMI telemetry. Processor vendors sell large dies as lower-core-count parts by
> disabling cores, defective or not, and do not publish which. This project shows the telemetry
> supercomputers already collect discloses it, and recovers the map for 1,962 POWER9 sockets of
> CINECA's Marconi100 from a public dataset.

## What it is

- m100-silicon-binning is an open-source analysis pipeline for recovering per-die CPU
  core-harvest maps from out-of-band BMC telemetry.
- It helps HPC operators and systems researchers see which cores are disabled on each individual
  processor die — information vendors do not publish.
- Use it when you have per-core sensor telemetry and want to detect latent hardware cohorts, infer
  processor replacements and moves without an asset database, or identify field core-guard events.
- It differs from PUF and hardware-fingerprinting work because it does not identify *which die* a
  part is; it recovers *what was disabled on it*, with no designed-in circuitry and no physical
  access.
- It is NOT a tool for reclaiming idle CPU cycles — that is the unrelated architectural sense of
  "core harvesting" — and it needs per-core sensors that are not renumbered, which not every BMC
  provides.

## How it works

A baseboard management controller exposes one thermal sensor per core position and does not
renumber the surviving cores compactly. A disabled core never emits a sample. So the
`pX_coreY_temp` metrics that never report mark the die's harvest map. If a BMC renumbered
survivors, every socket would report indices 0-15 and there would be one pattern; instead 443 of
495 possible patterns occur. The telemetry shows which positions are disabled, not why.

## Key findings

- Every map disables whole POWER9 slices (a core pair sharing L2/L3): 1,962 of 1,962 maps, no
  exception on 1.52 million clean socket-days, although POWER9 can disable single cores.
- The map is per-die, not per-SKU: 443 of 495 possible patterns observed.
- Harvested slices cluster, above all within POWER9 quads: 20 of 66 slice pairs are family-wise
  significant against 100,000 exchangeable curveball draws, and the six largest excesses are the
  six same-quad pairs, which IBM's chip diagram places side by side.
- The sensor index is IBM's core numbering. IBM's chip diagram places the quads in two bands of
  three; thermal coupling over 1,948 sockets confirms the quads but beyond them follows how the
  surviving cores are numbered, so the die layout rests on IBM's documentation, not on telemetry.
- A rack-aligned lot boundary at rack 22, most plausibly two procurement lots: permutation-calibrated
  p = 2.5e-4, and 47 of 49 held-out racks placed in their inferred lot.
- Configuration changes coincide with reboots, measured against an independent boot signal:
  126 of 132 transitions, against 47.6% expected from length-matched controls (the raw per-node-day
  reboot rate, 1.74%, is not the comparator: a transition spans a multi-day reporting gap); dated by
  boot epoch, 133 of 136 contain a boot and none is seen without one.
- Nine steady-state core-guard episodes, each matched by the operating system's CPU count, whose
  window brackets the sensor one, and beginning at a boot.
- Sockets change die at 2.1% per socket-year (rack-clustered 95% CI [1.6, 2.7]) with no asset
  database; 50 of the 96 changes are dies moved from another socket, so new processors enter at an
  inferred 1.0-1.2% per socket-year.
- The map does not usefully predict which dies get replaced: held-out risk-set concordance 0.55
  (95% CI [0.48, 0.61]) against a rack-permutation null of 0.50 +/- 0.04 (p = 0.12).
- Its association with socket power is bounded and small: +2.7, -1.5 and -1.0 W over each map
  summary's full range, 90% CIs within +/-5.6 W, against a +/-5 W margin (two of three equivalent).

## Cost of the disclosure, and what mitigates it

Exact recovery from a SINGLE 20-second sampling interval in 99.95% of socket-intervals, measured on
raw timestamps (collector gaps almost always silence whole sockets, not single cores). In a
degraded regime the knee is about seven surviving samples per core, half that for an attacker who
uses the pairing of cores into slices. There are no false positives, because a harvested core can
never emit a sample.

Mitigations that do NOT work: reducing sampling cadence (one 20 s slot in every six hours still
recovers every map from one day); deleting samples at random (independent deletion of 99.9% leaves
one-day exact recovery at 0.81, 0.9985 for a slice-aware attacker; at 99.99% one month still
recovers 0.99997, because maps are static and an attacker pools days).
Mitigations that DO work: publishing per-socket aggregates instead of per-core series; renumbering
survivors compactly to 0..n-1; per-node random renumbering only if redrawn for every release (a
fixed permutation is a fingerprint unique for about 99.7% of sockets). The channel is carried by
which sensors EXIST, not by what they report.

## Limitations

- Single system. Every result comes from Marconi100. Generalisation is untested and is the largest
  open weakness.
- Defect-driven versus policy-driven harvesting is NOT identified: both predict the clustering
  observed, and the fitted model cannot attribute it. The model is also misspecified.
- The lot boundary has no external confirmation from procurement records.
- Map-change classes (RELABEL, CPU-SWAP, NODE-SWAP) and the rates derived from them are inferred
  from telemetry, not verified against service records.
- The reliability null is bounded, not absolute: 85 replacement-consistent events exclude useful
  prediction by the map features but not a modest effect, and binary contrasts (slice-0 status,
  lot) up to about threefold remain possible.
- The novelty statement is an awareness claim, not a priority claim; the closest prior work is
  McCalpin's surveys of disabled cores on TACC's Stampede2 and Smith's reading of one POWER9 machine.
